newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway becomes net power importer in 1996 - report.
newsitem.headline: Norway becomes net power importer in 1996 - report.

text.p: Norway was short of electricity in 1996 and became a net buyer, importing almost nine terawatt hours (TWh) of power, preliminary figures from the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Administration (NVE) showed, according to Den norske stats oljeselskap AS (Statoil).
Sweden supplied 3.9 TWh and Denmark 4.6 TWh. Some of the Swedish supplies came from Denmark and Finland and were sold on to Norway, Statoil said.

Electricity prices in Norway, which relies exclusively on hydropower for electricity production, hit record highs last year due to lower water levels in the hydropower reservoirs and an extremely cold winter.

At the peak at the end of September the spot price on the Nord Pool electricity bourse hit 0.37 crowns per kilowatt hour (kWh). Nord Pool is a common electricity exchange between Sweden and Norway. Denmark and Finland plan to join at a later date.
This year prices have retreated back to around 0.12 crowns per kWh in March as reservoir water levels have returned to near normal and due to milder winter temperatures.
As prices have fallen Norway has resumed exporting power to Denmark. It still imports from Sweden due to the free trade across borders allowed by the common bourse.
The NVE figures showed Norwegian electricity consumption at 113 TWh in 1996, a decline of just over three TWh from 1995, largely due to reduced consumption by electricity boilers.
Domestic power generation in 1996 was below 105 TWh, compared with 123 TWh the year before.
